power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Target Trial Emulation of Metformin for Dementia Prevention in All of Us: Robustness to Cohort and Confounder Definitions

text.text: Metformin use has been associated with a lower risk of incident dementia than other antidiabetics.

We perform target trial emulation and causal competing risk analysis in the NIH All of Us (AoU) Research Program database, contrasting the effects of metformin and sulfonylurea initiation on dementia onset and death without dementia.

AoU's social and behavioral health data allowed us to test robustness to excluding such confounders, and we further adjusted for calendar year effects and prior antidiabetic exposure, using both semiparametric Cox proportional hazards (PH) models and nonparametric models.

Under stabilized inverse propensity score of treatment weighting, metformin was associated with a substantially lower risk of death (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.61, 95% CI: [0.49, 0.75]) and a lower incidence of dementia (HR: 0.90, 95% CI: [0.82, 1.02]).
Estimated HRs were closely aligned with estimates obtained in the UK primary care and US Mass General Brigham health systems.

This finding was robust to the inclusion of participants without a type 2 diabetes diagnosis at baseline and to the consideration of different covariate sets in the propensity score model, supporting metformin * These authors contributed equally as a promising candidate for dementia preven-28 tion and motivating prospective validation.
Drug repurposing offers a faster and cheaper route 39 to therapy than de-novo development.

The growing 40 availability of electronic health records (EHRs) en-41 ables analysis of drug exposure and disease trajec-42 tories in populations that may be more representa-43 tive than trial participants.

In this context, the tar-44 get trial emulation (TTE) framework (Hernán and 45 Robins, 2016) provides a powerful tool to design in-46 silico trials that combine the rigor of a randomized 47 controlled trial (RCT) with the long follow-up avail-48 able in observational studies. 45% of dementia risk has been attributed to modifiable risk factors, including type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Chatterjee et al., 2016; Livingston et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In this context, the tar-44 get trial emulation (TTE) framework <ref type="bibr">(Hernán and 45</ref> Robins, 2016) provides a powerful tool to design in-46 silico trials that combine the rigor of a randomized 47 controlled trial (RCT) with the long follow-up avail-48 able in observational studies. 45% of dementia risk has been attributed to modifiable risk factors, including type 2 diabetes (T2D) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Chatterjee et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Livingston et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Metformin, the first-line therapy for T2D, has been associated with extended lifetime and lower dementia incidence than placebo or other antidiabetics in observational studies and animal models.
Recently, its use has been extended beyond T2D, including preventatively in patients diagnosed with prediabetes.
A pilot RCT of short-acting metformin provided initial evidence of its efficacy in slowing cognitive decline in people with mild cognitive impairment without T2D (Luchsinger et al., 2016).
text.formatted: A pilot RCT of short-acting metformin provided initial evidence of its efficacy in slowing cognitive decline in people with mild cognitive impairment without T2D <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Luchsinger et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Whether these cognitive benefits hold in routine care data remains unclear. Charpignon et al. (2022) emulated a target trial to interrogate the effect of initiating metformin vs. an antidiabetic from the sulfonylurea drug class on dementia onset and competing death, using data from patients in the UK primary care and US Mass General Brigham (MGB) health systems.
text.formatted: Whether these cognitive benefits hold in routine care data remains unclear. <ref type="bibr">Charpignon et al. (2022)</ref> emulated a target trial to interrogate the effect of initiating metformin vs. an antidiabetic from the sulfonylurea drug class on dementia onset and competing death, using data from patients in the UK primary care and US Mass General Brigham (MGB) health systems.

text.text: A protective association was found for both outcomes.
However, important confounders such as lifestyle and socioeconomic factors were unmeasured and could not be taken into account.
Moreover, the representation of Black and Hispanic people was limited, and the tenyear study period excluded the COVID-19 pandemic.

We replicated this study design in the AoU Research Program, a large and diverse US cohort with rich survey data, social and behavioral information, a long follow-up allowing the evaluation of calendar year effects, and a sufficient sample size to stratify by T2D status.

Following the inverse propensity score of treatment weighting approach in Charpignon et al. (2022), we conducted causal analyses to investigate these aspects by restricting the population to participants with a T2D diagnosis at baseline and by enriching the propensity score model with calendar year of first prescription, lifestyle, education and socioeconomic variables, as well as prior history of other antidiabetic drug prescriptions.
text.formatted: Following the inverse propensity score of treatment weighting approach in <ref type="bibr">Charpignon et al. (2022)</ref>, we conducted causal analyses to investigate these aspects by restricting the population to participants with a T2D diagnosis at baseline and by enriching the propensity score model with calendar year of first prescription, lifestyle, education and socioeconomic variables, as well as prior history of other antidiabetic drug prescriptions.

text.text: We aim to provide insight into the potential benefits of metformin in the general adult population, and to assess the extent of balance between arms at baseline with respect to social and behavioral health factors often left unmeasured in prior studies, quantify their incremental contribution to confounding control, and evaluate the robustness of treatment effect estimates.
Design and data.
We emulated a target trial in AoU, comparing initiation of metformin vs. sulfonylureas on time to dementia onset, with death without dementia as a competing event.
We adapted the target trial emulation design of Charpignon et al. (2022), reusing their causalCmprsk estimator while refining eligibility criteria and extending the confounder set.
text.formatted: We adapted the target trial emulation design of <ref type="bibr">Charpignon et al. (2022)</ref>, reusing their causalCmprsk estimator while refining eligibility criteria and extending the confounder set.

text.text: Cohort.
Eligible participants were adults aged ≥50 at their first metformin or sulfonylurea prescription, defined as baseline.
At baseline, participants were required to have available sex at birth information, antidiabetic monotherapy, and no dementia diagnosis (Figure 1).
text.formatted: At baseline, participants were required to have available sex at birth information, antidiabetic monotherapy, and no dementia diagnosis (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants with chronic kidney disease (CKD) at baseline were excluded from both treatment arms because CKD may preclude metformin use (Imam, 2017) and therefore could determine treatment assignment.
text.formatted: Participants with chronic kidney disease (CKD) at baseline were excluded from both treatment arms because CKD may preclude metformin use <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Imam, 2017)</ref> and therefore could determine treatment assignment.

text.text: Applying this restriction also improved comparability of baseline kidney function between treatment arms.
We further restricted the cohort to include only participants with a T2D diagnosis at baseline, to obtain a more homogeneous cohort.
Arms were defined by the first prescription drug.
Drugs were mapped using ATC code, while dementia and comorbidities were defined from curated ICD/SNOMED code sets and drug lists when appropriate.
These appear in CSV files with the code.

As in Charpignon et al. (2022), the propensity score model included age at first prescription, sex at birth, race, ethnicity, baseline comorbidities (stroke, hypertension, obesity, CVD, cancer), and binned BMI and HbA1c, measured up to three years before baseline.
text.formatted: As in <ref type="bibr">Charpignon et al. (2022)</ref>, the propensity score model included age at first prescription, sex at birth, race, ethnicity, baseline comorbidities (stroke, hypertension, obesity, CVD, cancer), and binned BMI and HbA1c, measured up to three years before baseline.

text.text: Missing values were kept as explicit categories.

We additionally included calendar year of first prescription, binned into groups of 3-5 years to alleviate prescribing shifts, lifestyle factors (smoking and alcohol use), education information from AoU surveys, neighborhood-level zipcode-linked socioeconomic measures (Appendix B), and prior exposure to other antidiabetic drug classes (DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, insulin) since participants are not required to be treatmentnaive and prior use may proxy for diabetes severity or partial treatment history.

text.text: Cohort.
After excluding ineligible participants, our cohort comprised N =18,809 participants (metformin: N =16,449, sulfonylureas: N =2,360).

During follow-up, 2,900 dementia events (metformin: 2,422, sulfonylureas: 478) and 815 death events were recorded, including 225 deaths after dementia onset (metformin: 636 and 171, sulfonylureas: 179 and 54).

text.text: Treatment effect estimates.
As shown in Table 1, both weighting schemes shifted the estimated HR for dementia onset toward a similar protective effect (overlap: 0.92, [0.84, 1.02], stabilized ATE: 0.90, [0.82, 1.02]).
For competing death, metformin was protective under all weighting schemes (overlap: 0.67, [0.55, 0.81], stabilized ATE: 0.61, [0.49, 0.75]).
Compared to Charpignon et al. (2022) (dementia HR 0.81-0.86, death HR 0.57-0.66), the signal obtained for dementia onset is consistent but attenuated, while the competing death benefit is reproduced.

text.text: For both outcomes and all three weighting schemes, the nonparametric log HR curve tracked the constant HR within its 95% CI band through 15 years of follow-up (Figures 4, 5 and 6), supporting the PH assumption.

text.text: Some divergence appears beyond 15 years, in part because of a smaller number of participants.
The cumulative risk of dementia was estimated at 28-30% within 15 years of baseline, with metformin tracking below sulfonylureas by about 2% (Figure 7).

text.text: Throughout follow-up, the cumulative risk of death without dementia was substantially lower under metformin initiation than under sulfonylurea initiation (6% vs. 9% by year 15).
The dementia risk difference (Figure 8) was negative (favoring metformin initiation), with confidence intervals spanning zero, whereas the death risk difference remained negative.

Full unadjusted/overlap HRs for dementia and death and the corresponding cumulative risks, risk differences, and restricted mean time lost at different time points appear in Tables 10, 11, 12 and 13.

text.text: Restricting the cohort to participants with a T2D diagnosis thus strengthened the dementia signal slightly but left the mortality benefit unchanged.

Our target trial emulation in the NIH AoU database indicates that metformin initiation was robustly associated with a lower risk of death than sulfonylurea initiation in participants aged 50+ at baseline, irrespective of T2D status.
Our analysis also suggests a lower risk of dementia onset under metformin initiation, although the HR estimate was borderline significant.

Results obtained in this large and diverse US cohort corroborate a study conducted in the UK primary care and MGB health systems (Charpignon et al., 2022), as HR estimates closely aligned for dementia onset (UK=0.86, MGB=0.81, AoU=0.90) and death (UK=0.66, MGB=0.57, AoU=0.61).

text.text: Notably, the beneficial effect of metformin initiation was slightly larger when restricting the population to participants with a coded T2D diagnosis (HR death=0.61 vs.
0.63, HR dementia onset=0.90 vs.

Importantly, available AoU data for social and behavioral health variables mentioned as unmeasured confounders in previous work allowed us to test whether estimated propensity scores, HRs, and cumulative risks were sensitive to their inclusion.
While all estimates were robust in our study, in part because the baseline distributions of these variables were quite balanced between arms, this observation may not hold in other datasets.
In contrast, including the calendar year of first prescription yielded slightly different propensity scores (up to ±0.25), lower HR and higher risk difference estimates.
This finding underscores the importance of accounting for calendar year patterns to reduce residual confounding, especially when the study period spans multiple decades.
Indeed, clinical guidelines change over time, influencing physician prescribing preferences.
Additionally, mortality rates and dementia incidence rates exhibit both birth cohort effects and secular trends.
Our study has several limitations. (i) The setting (e.g., outpatient vs. inpatient) corresponding to the first prescription was lacking for a sizable proportion of participants.

This may result in the mixture of participants who received a prescription to treat chronic T2D with others who experienced a transient hyperglycemic event. (ii) We estimated the intention-to-treat effect of metformin on dementia onset, in the presence of competing death.
However, participants are likely to switch to another antidiabetic monotherapy if they experience side effects or to a polytherapy if their T2D deteriorates.

Therefore, a per-protocol analysis that accounts for changes in antidiabetic drug exposure and handles time-varying confounders is warranted. (iii) Given the prevalence of missing data, future work could also explore different data imputation schemes. (iv) Our estimates rely on the correct specification of the propensity score model.

Future analyses could include dementia and death outcome models and use a doubly-robust approach (e.g., survival targeted maximum likelihood estimation (Benkeser and Hejazi, 2020)) to derive corresponding cumulative risks. (v) The timing of treatment initiation may be inexact, as suggested by a larger-than-expected prevalence of prior insulin prescriptions at baseline.
text.formatted: Future analyses could include dementia and death outcome models and use a doubly-robust approach (e.g., survival targeted maximum likelihood estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Benkeser and Hejazi, 2020)</ref>) to derive corresponding cumulative risks. (v) The timing of treatment initiation may be inexact, as suggested by a larger-than-expected prevalence of prior insulin prescriptions at baseline.

text.text: To alleviate this issue, we could learn a latent T2D status or a baseline shift parameter for each participant based on other information in their EHR (e.g., health visits, drug prescriptions, medical exams).
Similarly, the diagnosis of dementia is often delayed and only approximate.
Our outcome models could be adapted to accommodate such interval-censored data.

Going forward, it would be of interest to replicate our approach in additional health databases (e.g., Kaiser Permanente, FinnGen) to strengthen evidence, assess the repurposing potential of metformin with greater precision, test for effect heterogeneity, and understand underlying mechanisms via mediation analyses.
Of the 481,919 participants with EHR data, 400,846 had no metformin or sulfonylurea prescription and were excluded, leaving 61,209 metformin and 19,864 sulfonylurea arm participants.

We then applied the eligibility criteria sequentially: restricting to one drug at initiation and including in each arm only participants whose first recorded prescription corresponded to that arm's drug removed 10,248 metformin and 13,879 sulfonylurea initiators; requiring age ≥ 50 at first prescription removed 18,421 metformin and 1,927 sulfonylurea initiators; excluding a dementia diagnosis at or before baseline removed 1,880 and 156 metformin and sulfonylurea initiators, respectively; excluding a chronic kidney disease (CKD) diagnosis at or before baseline, a metformin contraindication (Imam, 2017), removed 1,162 and 432; and requiring available sex at birth information removed 122 and 30 metformin and sulfonylurea initiators, respectively.

These steps yield the unrestricted ("No T2D restriction") cohort of 29,376 metformin and 3,440 sulfonylurea initiators used in the sensitivity analysis presented in the "T2D ascertainment" paragraph of Section 3 and in Appendix D.4.

Finally, restricting to participants with a T2D diagnosis at or before baseline removed 12,927 metformin and 1,080 sulfonylurea initiators, producing the primary cohort of 16,449 metformin and 2,360 sulfonylurea initiators.

Within this cohort, 2,422 dementia events and 636 deaths (of which 171 occurred after dementia onset) were observed in the metformin arm, 469 and 478 dementia events and 179 deaths (54 after de-470 mentia onset) in the sulfonylurea arm.

Sensitivity analysis: removing covariates from the propensity score Prescription year shift As show in Figure 11, incident prescriptions of both drugs rose from a few prescriptions per year before 2000 to a peak of 1,506 metformin and 176 sulfonylurea initiations in 2019 and 2018, respectively, before declining through 2020-2024, consistent with pandemic related disruption to routine primary care.

The composition also shifted over time: the metformin-to-sulfonylureas ratio among incident prescriptions rose from roughly 1.5:1 in the early 2000s to approx. 6:1 by the mid-2010s and 10-15:1 by 2019-2024, consistent with clinical guidelines recommending metformin as the firstline antidiabetic therapy.

This temporal structure likely also reflects the All of Us Research Program's recruitment trajectory (enrollment grew rapidly from 2018 onward, drawing on a mix of retrospective and prospective EHR data).
Sensitivity analysis results Dropping prescription year from the propensity score model had the highest effect on the results in our sensitivity analyses.
It attenuated the weighted death HR towards the null under both overlap (0.67 → 0.82) and stabilized ATE (0.61 → 0.75) weighting, and the dementia HR as well (0.90-0.92 → 0.99; Table 4).

text.text: The five neighborhood-level covariates are derived by linking each participant's residential ZIP code (ZIP Code Tabulation Area, ZCTA) to American Community Survey estimates, and describe the participant's local area rather than the individual socioeconomic information.

Each is defined as follows: • Assisted income (% of ZIP code): the percentage of households in the ZIP code receiving public assistance income (e.g., cash publicassistance or Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)/food-stamp benefits).
• High-school education (% of ZIP code): the percentage of adults (aged ≥ 25 years) in the ZIP code who have attained at least a highschool diploma or equivalent.
• Median household income ($): the median annual household income (in US dollars) across households in the ZIP code.
• No health insurance (% of ZIP code): the percentage of the civilian noninstitutionalized population in the ZIP code without any health insurance coverage.
• Poverty (% of ZIP code): the percentage of the population in the ZIP code with income below the federal poverty line.
All five measures were standardized to zero mean and unit variance, and missing values were medianimputed, as described in the "Confounders" paragraph of Section 2.

text.text: Effect estimation.
Baseline randomization was emulated via inverse propensity score of treatment weighting.
Logistic regression was used to estimate propensity scores.
Our main analysis focused on the average treatment effect (ATE) as the causal estimand of interest and used stabilized ATE weights.
Our secondary analysis considered the average treatment effect in the overlap population (ATO) as the estimand and involved overlap weights.
Covariate balance before vs. after weighting was assessed via absolute standardized mean differences (threshold 0.1, following the literature's convention).

Under each weighting scheme, we estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and cumulative risks of dementia onset and death without dementia, both nonparametrically and via cause-specific Cox PH models, using causalCmprsk with a Bayesian bootstrap for uncertainty estimation (1,000 replicates).
For the two competing events, we additionally derived time-varying risk differences and the restricted mean time lost or gained due to treatment, following the definitions in Vakulenko-Lagun et al.
(2023); Charpignon et al.
Robustness scenarios.

Beyond the primary analysis, we performed five sensitivity analyses: (i) the choice of balancing weights (stabilized ATE vs. overlap); (ii) incremental contribution of calendar year of first prescription; (iii) incremental contribution of lifestyle covariates; (iv) incremental contribution of educational attainment and neighborhood characteristics information; and (v) including all initiators regardless of a coded T2D diagnosis, while adding it as a comorbidity.
Consideration (v) highlights an improvement over
Contribution of individual confounders.
Enriching the propensity score model variably affected arm separation (Figure 10).

The distribution of the calendar year of first prescription showed a marked temporal structure both overall volume and by treatment arm (Figure 11), consistent with clinical guidelines recommending metformin as the firstline antidiabetic therapy in 2006 (Nathan et al., 2006), pandemic-related disruptions to routine primary care, and the AoU Research Program's rapid enrollment from 2018 onward.
While the observed calendar-year pattern conflates true practice shifts for cumulative risks, risk differences, and restricted mean time lost at different time points).

In contrast, the two lifestyle covariates (smoking, alcohol use) and the combined educational attainment and neighborhood-level characteristics affected the propensity score to a smaller extent and did not change the magnitude and significance of estimated treatment effects.
